edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἑαυτῷ δὲ λαμβάνει Κέλσος ὅτι ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην καὶ ἀστέρας ἡγούμεθα εἶναι τὸ μηδέν. περὶ ὧν ὁμολογοῦμεν ὅτι καὶ αὐτοὶ „τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τῶν υἱῶν τοῦ θεοῦ“ ἀπεκδέχονται, „τῇ“ τῶν ὑλικῶν σωμάτων „ματαιότητι“ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ὑποτεταγμένοι, „διὰ τὸν ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι ὑποτάξαντα.“ εἰ δ᾿ ἀνεγνώκει ὁ Κέλσος καὶ ἄλλα μὲν μυρία. ὅσα περὶ ἡλίου καὶ σελήνης καὶ ἄστρων φαμὲν, καὶ τὸ „αἰνεῖτε αὐτὸν πάντα τὰ ἄστρα καὶ τὸ φῶς“ καὶ τὸ „αἰνεῖτε αὐτὸν οἱ οὐρανοὶ τῶν οὐρανῶν,“ οὐκ ἂν περὶ ἡμῶν ἀπεφήνατο ὅτι λέγομεν τὰ τηλικαῦτα, αἰνοῦντα μεγάλως τὸν θεὸν, εἶναι τὸ μηδέν. οὐκ οἶδε δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος οὐδὲ τὸ „ἡ γὰρ ἀποκαραδοκία τῆς κτίσεως τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τῶν υἱῶν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπεκδέχεται. τῇ γὰρ ματαιότητι ἡ κτίσις ὑπετάγη, οὐχ ἑκοῦσα, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα, ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι, ὅτι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ κτίσις ἐλευθερωθήσεται ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς φθορᾶς εἰς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τῆς δόξης τῶν τέκνων τοῦ θεοῦ.“ καὶ ἐν τούτοις δὴ τέλος ἐχέτω ἡ περὶ τοῦ μὴ σέβειν ἡμᾶς ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην καὶ ἀστέρας ἀπολογία. ἐκθώμεθα δὲ καὶ τὴν ἑξῆς λέξιν, ἵνα μετὰ τοῦτο πρὸς αὐτὴν θεοῦ διδόντος εἴπωμεν τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας φωτὸς δοθησόμενα ἡμῖν.
thought_title: The stars await the freedom of God’s children
pass_a_gloss: Celsus takes for himself (ἑαυτῷ λαμβάνει) that we consider sun, moon and stars to be nothing (τὸ μηδέν). Concerning which we confess (ὁμολογοῦμεν) that they too await (ἀπεκδέχονται) 'the revelation (ἀποκάλυψιν) of the sons of God', for the present subjected (ὑποτεταγμένοι) 'to the futility (ματαιότητι)' of material (ὑλικῶν) bodies, 'because of him who subjected them in hope.' But if Celsus had read the myriad other things we say about sun, moon and stars, and the 'praise (αἰνεῖτε) him, all the stars and the light' and 'praise him, heavens of the heavens', he would not have declared (ἀπεφήνατο) about us that we say such great things, greatly praising God, are nothing. Nor does Celsus know the 'for the eager expectation (ἀποκαραδοκία) of the creation (κτίσεως) awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willing (ἑκοῦσα), but because of the one who subjected it, in hope, that the creation itself also will be freed (ἐλευθερωθήσεται) from the slavery (δουλείας) of corruption (φθορᾶς) into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.' And in these let the defence (ἀπολογία) about our not revering (σέβειν) sun, moon and stars have its end. Let us set out (ἐκθώμεθα) also the next passage (λέξιν), so that after this, God giving, we may say against it the things to be given us from the light of truth.

choices.why: ὅτι states the content of the hope

pass_b_english: Celsus takes it for granted that we hold the sun, the moon and the stars to be “nothing”. About them we confess that they too wait for “the revelation of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19), being subjected for the present to “the futility” of material bodies “because of him who subjected them in hope” (Romans 8:20).

If Celsus had read the countless other things we say about the sun, the moon and the stars, and the words “Praise him, all you stars and light” (Psalm 148:3) and “Praise him, you heavens of heavens” (Psalm 148:4), he would not have declared of us that we say these great beings, which praise God greatly, are “nothing”. Nor does Celsus know the words: “For the eager longing of the creation waits for the revelation of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself also will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:19–21).

With this, then, let our defence for not revering the sun, the moon and the stars come to an end. Let us also set out his next passage, so that afterwards, God granting, we may say in reply to it whatever will be given us from the light of the truth.
notes: 'Nothing' (τὸ μηδέν) is Celsus's word from his passage in 5.6, so it is quoted. In the first allusion to Romans 8:20 Origen inserts 'of material bodies' between the quoted words and applies the passage to the heavenly bodies; the plural ('them') follows his adaptation. Psalm 148:3–4: LXX and English numbering agree; the LXX 'all the stars and the light' differs from the Hebrew 'all you stars of light'. Origen's view that the stars are living, rational beings (cf. 5.10) is kept as he states it.

changes: Romans 8:20-21 ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι, ὅτι: 'in hope; because the creation' changed to 'in hope that the creation' (ὅτι states the content of the hope)
Checked: τὸ μηδέν is Celsus's word in 5.6 (quoted correctly); Psalm 148:3-4 LXX numbering equals English; Romans 8:19-21 wording verified; no omissions
